Brussels, Belgium

Brussels halves its growth forecast for France to 0.4% in 2026 and sees it last in the eurozone in 2027, with 9.2% unemployment

On Tuesday, November 17, the European Commission cut its forecasts for France: 0.4% growth in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027, down from 0.8% and 1.1% in the spring. The deficit would stay at 5.4% of GDP in 2027, above the government's target, while the eurozone is speeding up [1][2][3].
Brussels raised its forecast for the eurozone as a whole to 1.2% growth in 2026, up from 0.9% before, but sharply downgraded its forecast for France [1][4].
At 0.6% in 2027, France would have the weakest growth in the eurozone. Yet its 2027 budget is based on 1% growth next year [2].
The public deficit would reach 5.5% of GDP in 2026 and 5.4% in 2027, compared with an average of 3.6% in the eurozone. The government is aiming for 5% in 2027 [2][3].
Public debt would rise from 119.2% of GDP this year to 122.1% in 2027, then 123.2% in 2028. Interest payments would climb from 2.2% of GDP in 2025 to 3% in 2027 [3].
Unemployment would rise from 8.4% in 2026 to 9.2% in 2027, then 9.8% in 2028, compared with 6.5% expected in the eurozone in 2027 [3][2].
Brussels points to higher energy prices, weak investment, especially in housing, and the impact of this summer's droughts and heatwaves on farm output [3].

Valdis Dombrovskis, the Commissioner for the Economy, noted “a sharp rise in borrowing rate spreads” for France and Belgium, and said it was essential for deficits and debt to start falling again, while seeing “no imminent problem” for financial stability [4][5].
Key takeaway: Brussels is much less optimistic than the government, whose 2027 budget is built on 1% growth next year, and France is falling behind while its neighbors speed up [2][1].
Less growth means less tax revenue. If the economy grows more slowly than expected, the goal of a 5% deficit in 2027 becomes harder to reach without new spending cuts or tax hikes [2][3].

Rising interest rates also weigh in: when the state pays more to borrow, the cost of the debt grows and eats into the budget's room for maneuver, hence Valdis Dombrovskis's warning about France's rate spread [3][4].

These figures come as the 2027 budget is being debated in Parliament. The Commission is due to publish its detailed budget recommendations next week, and is already calling on France and Belgium to fix their public finances [4][5].

If you're looking for a job, the forecast of 9.2% unemployment in 2027 points to a tougher market, especially for people entering the workforce. If you have a variable-rate mortgage or plan to buy a home, higher government borrowing rates can feed into the rates banks charge.

Ukraine: a span of the Crimean Bridge collapses into the sea after a weeks-long operation, Moscow strikes back at Kyiv's bridges on the eve of Berlin talks

On Tuesday, November 17, after a second night of Ukrainian strikes, the road span of the Crimean Bridge, which links Russia to the occupied peninsula, fell into the Kerch Strait. Zelensky describes a seven-stage operation prepared over several weeks. The same day, Russian missiles hit two major bridges in Kyiv [1][2][3][5].

The Ukrainian security service (SBU) says a steel arch and the roadway beneath it are “completely destroyed,” and that the railway section is also damaged [2]. Images show the 227-meter road span in the water, while the rail span is still standing [9].

Volodymyr Zelensky describes a seven-phase operation carried out over “several weeks”: first destroying air defenses, radars and jammers, then striking with drones and Flamingo and Neptune missiles [3].

Crimea's Moscow-appointed head, Sergei Aksyonov, announced that traffic was suspended [4]. Russia's Transport Ministry later reopened rail traffic on a single track, with repairs continuing on the other [2][4].
The 19 km bridge has already been hit by Ukraine at least three times [2][3]. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov says it will be repaired and come out stronger than before [9].

In response, Russia targeted Kyiv's North and South bridges over the Dnipro. Seven ballistic missiles, according to Zelensky [10], left neighborhoods without water and power and killed at least two people [5].
On Thursday, November 19, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet Ukrainians and Europeans in Berlin, but the Kremlin says it has not agreed to the Europeans taking part [11][12].

Key takeaway: this is the hardest blow to the bridge since the war began. The trucks supplying Crimea and the southern front with fuel, ammunition and equipment no longer have a direct road, and if the span has to be replaced, repairs could take a long time [1][7]. One engineer estimates it would take more than a year to restore all road traffic [6].

There is also an impact at sea. The span fell into the channel linking the Sea of Azov to the Black Sea, and its debris could block large ships [1][6]. For Andrey Sizov of the consultancy Sovecon, this could delay the resumption of exports from Azov ports, which reopened to grain ships in late October [7].

The symbolism matters as much as the logistics: Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and this bridge embodies its control over the peninsula [2]. According to the Institute for the Study of War, Kyiv is trying to cut the main Russian supply routes running through Crimea [2].

The timing is no coincidence. The strike comes two days before Vladimir Putin meets Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen [6], and the Kremlin does not rule out a link with the upcoming talks [9]. Ukraine's foreign minister, Andriy Sybiha, fears this summit will encourage Putin to keep going [8].

For you, the direct impact is limited: if the channel stays blocked, Russian grain exports from the Sea of Azov may be delayed [7]. Above all, this “war of the bridges” weighs on Thursday's meetings in Berlin and Shenzhen [6][11].

Shenzhen, China

Mexico: in Shenzhen, Sheinbaum offers Xi Jinping a “new era” with China despite her tariffs, before crossing paths with Trump

On Tuesday, November 17 in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met Xi Jinping for the first time since taking office. She wants to sell more to China and open a “new era,” even though Mexico has been taxing Chinese goods at up to 50% since January [2][3][7].
The meeting took place on the afternoon of November 17, with Cai Qi, top diplomat Wang Yi and Huang Kunming on the Chinese side, according to Beijing's readout [1].
Claudia Sheinbaum described a “cordial and frank” exchange and proposed opening a “new era” in relations between the two countries [3][8].
She wants to boost Mexican exports to China, citing avocados and tequila, especially in the agri-food sector [5].

The two leaders talked about a new stage of cooperation in trade, technology, clean energy and science. Sheinbaum also asked for investment, help against sargassum (seaweed that floods Caribbean beaches) and cooperation on AI [6].
She asked for a giant panda for the Chapultepec Zoo in Mexico City [4]. She also invited Xi Jinping to the 2028 APEC summit, which Mexico will host [8].
According to Bloomberg, the aim was to turn the page on a recent trade dispute without irritating the United States [2]. Xi Jinping stressed the importance of stable relations [1].
Key takeaway: Mexico is trying to open up more to China without angering its main partner, the United States. It's a tricky balance, since the dispute is recent [2][7].

Mexico's Congress passed tariffs of up to 50% on more than 1,400 products from China and other countries without a free trade agreement with Mexico. In force since January, they target cars, auto parts, textiles, footwear and household appliances [10][7]. China's Commerce Ministry asked Mexico to correct these “unilateralist and protectionist” practices as soon as possible [7].

The stakes are high: China is Mexico's second-largest supplier after the United States, with more than $100 billion in trade a year since 2023 [7]. Washington is pushing Sheinbaum to rein in Chinese industry based in Mexico; she denies any link between her tariffs and talks with the Americans [7].

Meanwhile, Donald Trump is threatening to double his tariffs on Mexico over a migrant caravan. Sheinbaum, who also met Mark Carney in Shenzhen, was due to meet Trump briefly on Wednesday, November 18 at the APEC summit [9][3]. The three countries are renegotiating their North American free trade agreement [3].

For you, this is an example of how countries caught between Washington and Beijing try to play both sides. Mexico is the workshop for many factories that supply the United States, including European groups (cars, parts). If trade tensions rise between these three countries, these companies' prices and supply chains feel it [7][10].

news.2026-11-18-irak-oleoduc-turquie.tit: Iraq: to bypass Hormuz, Baghdad reopens its pipeline to Turkey, shut for 12 years because of the Islamic State
news.2026-11-18-irak-oleoduc-turquie.sum: On Tuesday, November 17, Iraq resumed pumping oil for export through its old pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan, idle since 2014. The flow starts at 120,000 barrels a day and is set to rise to 500,000. A few hours later, the government approved the pipeline's rehabilitation [1][2].
news.2026-11-18-irak-oleoduc-turquie.poi: Iraq's oil minister announced on Tuesday the resumption of crude pumping for export to Turkey, at an initial rate of 120,000 barrels a day, set to gradually climb to 500,000 barrels a day [1][2].
No timeline was given for reaching full capacity [2]. The effect on Iraq's total exports will depend on the volumes available and on whether they add to current deliveries or not [1].
The same day, the Council of Ministers approved a recommendation to rehabilitate the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, a few hours after announcing that flows had resumed, a first in 12 years [2].
Pumping had been halted in 2014 after a series of attacks on the pipeline by Islamic State fighters [3].
Baghdad and Ankara signed a one-year agreement to keep oil flowing through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, with a transport capacity of up to 750,000 barrels a day, pending a long-term deal [4][5].

Oil relations between the two countries are still marked by a dispute: in March 2023, an International Chamber of Commerce arbitration ruled that Turkey had breached its agreement with Iraq by letting through Kurdish oil exported without Baghdad's approval [4].
news.2026-11-18-irak-oleoduc-turquie.why: Key takeaway: in the middle of the war around Iran, Iraq is giving its oil a northern exit that depends neither on its southern terminals nor on the Strait of Hormuz [2][5].

Until now, Iraq relied on its southern oil terminals on the Gulf. To get out, tankers have to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupted by the war with Iran. Every barrel sent north to Turkey avoids this risky passage [2][5].

The stakes go beyond Iraq: oil arriving in Ceyhan, on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, no longer has to cross the Gulf. With a planned capacity of up to 750,000 barrels a day under the deal with Ankara, the route could become a real safety valve if the strait closes again [4][5].
The route remains fragile: it crosses areas long targeted by armed groups, and the sharing of oil with the autonomous Kurdistan region has not been settled, as the 2023 arbitration showed [3][4].
news.2026-11-18-irak-oleoduc-turquie.for: The more routes there are to get oil out of the Middle East without going through Hormuz, the less a crisis in the strait sends the price of a barrel soaring, and with it the cost of filling your tank. On top of that, Iraqi oil arriving in Ceyhan, on the Mediterranean, is much closer to Europe than the Gulf terminals.

Australia: Albanese arrives in China with the heads of BHP and Rio Tinto, just as Beijing tightens its grip on iron ore

On Wednesday, November 18, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrived in Shenzhen for the APEC summit, accompanied by top business leaders including the heads of BHP and Rio Tinto. The day before, the Sydney stock market fell 1.8%, dragged down by miners, as China's state iron ore buyer takes a harder line in negotiations [1][4][5].
Albanese landed on Wednesday in Shenzhen, in southern China, for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which China is hosting this year [4][7].

He is due to meet President Xi Jinping there on Friday, on the sidelines of the summit: it will be their fifth official meeting. He will then meet Premier Li Qiang in Beijing for their annual meeting [3].

According to Reuters, Albanese and 11 top executives, including Matt Holcz, head of iron ore at Rio Tinto, and Geraldine Slattery, head of BHP Australia, will take part with Li Qiang in the 9th Australia-China CEO Roundtable, co-hosted by the Business Council of Australia and the China Development Bank [1][2].

In the background: China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG), the state buyer that centralizes Chinese ore purchases, asked steel mills this year not to buy certain cargoes from BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue during annual negotiations [1].
BHP and Rio Tinto eventually signed new contracts; Fortescue is still negotiating and warns that its business could suffer without a deal by the end of the year [1][2].

On Tuesday, November 17, the ASX 200 index lost 1.79% to 8,883.2 points. BHP fell about 5%, Rio Tinto 2.1% and Fortescue 5.6%, following the ore price in Singapore [5]. Iron ore futures fell to their lowest level in four years [6].
Key takeaway: Australia relies heavily on its iron ore sales to China, and Beijing now uses a single buyer to put pressure on prices. Albanese's trip is also about defending his miners [1][2].

By pooling purchases in CMRG, China gains bargaining power: facing a single giant customer, miners have less leeway to set their prices [1]. Resources Minister Madeleine King said she was worried that contracts signed with CMRG would weigh on miners' profits [5].

Canberra has already warned publicly that manipulating this trade could breach international rules, while trying to stabilize the relationship [1]. Asked about the issue, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia would keep defending its interests [7].

The context is delicate: Albanese is arriving from Manila, where he agreed with Donald Trump, India's Narendra Modi and Japan's Sanae Takaichi to expand the Quad's military cooperation. He says he does not fear Chinese retaliation [3].

For you, the effect is indirect: iron ore is used to make the steel in your car, your household appliances or buildings. A price at its lowest in four years [6] eases costs for steelmakers, but also shows that Chinese industry is slowing down. If you have money in commodity funds, BHP and Rio Tinto often make up a big share of them [5].

news.2026-11-18-fin-deutsche-bank-fuite-: Frankfurt, Germany
Germany
Deutsche Bank shares fall 6% after a leak of 15 million internal documents on Epstein, Trump and Russia

On Tuesday, November 17, Deutsche Bank lost 6% in Frankfurt, closing at 30.94 euros, its worst session since April 2025. The cause: an investigation by more than 200 journalists based on 15 million internal documents. The bank says the events are old, while Berlin demands “transparency” [1][2][3].

The documents, including emails and meeting minutes, were obtained by two journalists, one in India and the other in South Africa, then analyzed by a consortium of more than 200 journalists, including the Financial Times and The New York Times [1]. The investigation is coordinated by the South African NGO Barracuda Media [4].

According to the Financial Times, the bank processed more suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein than previously known, totaling $582 million. It also allegedly sent a Donald Trump tax document by mistake to another client's accountant in 2017 [1][5].

According to The New York Times, Deutsche Bank was still seeking to grow in Russia in 2021 [1]. Its CEO, Christian Sewing, was part of the working group that prepared this strategy, according to the consortium's media outlets [6].

The stock fell as much as 6.4% during the session [7] before closing down 6.0% at 30.94 euros. It was the biggest drop on the DAX, Frankfurt's benchmark index, that day [2]. Reuters notes that it could not immediately verify the published information [1].
The bank says the events “date back many years, in some cases up to two decades,” and says it spent 7 billion euros between 2019 and 2025 to strengthen its controls [4][8].

Lars Klingbeil, Germany's finance minister, is asking the bank for “full transparency” on how it fixed its past failings. He is leaving the investigation to regulators and the courts. BaFin, Germany's financial watchdog, notes that it has carried out six investigations into Deutsche Bank since 2018 [8].
Key takeaway: Germany's largest bank, which had put its scandals behind it, is seeing its past resurface, and its shareholders wiped 6% off its value in a single session [2][3].
The drop came on an already dark day: the Stoxx 600, an index of 600 large European companies, lost 1.75%, its worst session since March 20, dragged down by fears about AI [2].

Investors are mainly worried about what comes next: investigations, fines, executive departures. According to Handelsblatt, the documents show that the bank neglected its anti-money laundering and high-risk client controls for years [9]. Christian Sewing acknowledged that mistakes had been made under his leadership; the chairman of the supervisory board defended him [6].
This is not the first leak: in 2020, the “FinCEN Files” already named Deutsche Bank more than any other bank, and its shares fell the same day [10][11].

Not a Deutsche Bank customer? If you have a fund or an ETF tracking large European companies, it is probably part of it, like other banks. These scandals are also a reminder of why your bank asks where the money comes from for a large transfer: those anti-money laundering checks are what is at issue here.

How it works: why an old scandal can sink a bank's shares today

A share price reflects the profits investors expect in the future. A leak about past events can lead to future costs: regulatory investigations, fines, legal fees, lost customers. The market doesn't yet know how much all this will cost, so it sells as a precaution: it's the uncertainty that drives the price down, more than the facts themselves. For a bank, the risk is twofold: a big fine reduces its capital, the cushion that allows it to lend, and the regulator can impose more costly controls. That's why Deutsche Bank stresses the 7 billion euros already spent on controls [4]: it wants to convince people that the bill for the past has been paid. When a fine is finally known and quantified, the stock can actually rise, because the doubt disappears.
Precedents: Deutsche Bank and its scandals
September 2016

The US Justice Department demands $14 billion from Deutsche Bank over its mortgage-backed securities; the stock plunges 8% [12] and then hits a record low of 10.62 euros on September 26 [13]. The bank calls it an “opening position” and expects a “significantly lower” amount [13].
An unknown fine is scary: the stock had by then lost more than 65% since its July 2015 peak [14].
January 2017
Deutsche Bank agrees to pay about $628 million in fines over a Russian “mirror trading” scheme involving $10 billion [15]. The stock gains 1% to 18.82 euros on the day of the announcement [16].
Once the penalty is known, the doubt disappears: the market breathes easier, even if the fine is heavy [16].
September 21, 2020

The “FinCEN Files,” some 2,100 suspicious activity reports, name Deutsche Bank in connection with $1.3 trillion in dubious flows, more than any other bank. Its shares fall as much as 8.6% in Frankfurt [10][11].
Shares of major global banks plunged that day: a massive leak can trigger selling across the whole sector, not just the bank in question [11].

news.2026-11-18-canada-macklem-depart-ba: Canada: Tiff Macklem will step down as head of the central bank in June 2027, the search for a successor begins

On Monday, November 16, the Bank of Canada announced that its governor, Tiff Macklem, will not seek a second term. He will leave at the end of his seven-year term, on June 2, 2027. A committee will look for his successor, with a choice expected in spring 2027 [1][2].

The Zurich-based recruitment firm Egon Zehnder will assist the bank's board of directors. The final decision will rest with Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne [1][2].
The announcement comes a few weeks after a rate hike to 2.5%, the first in more than three years [1].
An expected departure: Tiff Macklem is 65, and no governor has served a second term since 1980, Reuters notes [1].
He describes his term as unfolding in “a more fragmented and shock-prone world” [2].
Key takeaway: Canada will change central bank chiefs in the middle of a trade war with the United States, just as the bank has started raising rates again [1].

According to economists quoted by CBC, Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers would on paper be a strong candidate; she would become the first woman in the job. But the last four governors, since 2001, came from outside the bank [2].
For you, the effect is indirect: the governor sets the cost of borrowing in Canada and influences the Canadian dollar. If you have plans in Canada, this is a name to watch in the spring [1][2].

news.2026-11-18-allemagne-zew-moral-inve: Germany: investor morale jumps to 35.6 points, its highest since the war with Iran began

On Tuesday, November 17, the ZEW index, which measures what investors expect from the German economy over the next six months, rose to 35.6 points, up from 28.1 in October. That's well above the 28.8 expected by economists, and the highest level since the war with Iran began [1][2].
None of the economists surveyed by Bloomberg had forecast such a high figure [1].
The assessment of the current situation remains very negative, though it is improving: -33.2 points, compared with -35.9 the previous month [1][3].
Across the eurozone, expectations also improved, from 18.5 to 26.5 points [1][3].
ZEW President Achim Wambach believes the German economy “remains on the path to recovery, but at a slow pace” [3].

Key takeaway: investors are betting on a rebound in Europe's largest economy, but they still find the current situation bad. The ZEW cites two possible sources of support: more industrial orders and cheaper oil [3].

Germany has almost stagnated for three years. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel expects stronger growth in the fourth quarter, supported by defense and infrastructure spending, while warning that the recovery is not yet broad-based [4].
Germany is France's biggest customer. If its economy picks up, French companies that sell it parts, machinery or farm products benefit, and so do jobs.

news.2026-11-18-inde-cyclone-akvan.title: India: Cyclone Akvan set to hit Andhra Pradesh on Friday, Odisha begins evacuations and mobilizes 74 rescue teams
news.2026-11-18-inde-cyclone-akvan.summa: Cyclone Akvan is strengthening in the Bay of Bengal. According to India's national weather service, it is expected to hit the coast of Andhra Pradesh on November 20, with winds of 120 to 130 km/h. The neighboring state of Odisha began evacuating the most exposed residents on Tuesday, November 17 [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-18-inde-cyclone-akvan.point: It is the third cyclone of the season to target Andhra Pradesh, after Arnab and Murasu [1].
The weather service (IMD) expects Akvan to make landfall between Nellore and Tuni around noon on November 20, and to become a “severe cyclone” by Tuesday evening [1][3].
Odisha is deploying 74 rescue teams (60 from the state, 14 from the national force) and ordering evacuations in six southern districts, including Ganjam, Gajapati and Koraput [2].
Andhra Pradesh is on red alert and fishermen are banned from going out to sea [2].
news.2026-11-18-inde-cyclone-akvan.why.0: Key takeaway: Akvan is already the third cyclone of the season on this coast. Odisha isn't waiting for it to make landfall to evacuate and pre-position its rescue teams [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-18-inde-cyclone-akvan.why.1: The heavy rain won't hit only Andhra Pradesh: Odisha and Tamil Nadu are also getting ready [2][3]. These farming and coastal states face the risk of flooding and damaged crops.
news.2026-11-18-inde-cyclone-akvan.forMe: If you're planning a trip to southeastern India this week, expect canceled flights and trains. Otherwise, the impact on your daily life will be small.

news.2026-11-18-maroc-budget-2027-consei: Morocco: the 2027 budget goes before the upper house, with lower income tax and a 40% corporate tax for oil companies

After its adoption by members of the House of Representatives on November 14, Morocco's draft 2027 budget was presented on Tuesday, November 17 to the finance committee of the House of Councillors, the second chamber of Parliament, by Minister Fouzi Lekjaa [1][2].
Members of the lower house adopted it at first reading by 179 votes to 126, with no abstentions [2].
The threshold at which people start paying income tax would rise from 40,000 to 60,000 dirhams a year [1].
Fuel importers and distributors earning at least 100 million dirhams would see their corporate tax rise from 35% to 40% [1].
The opposition criticizes how the budget is financed and the postponement of several reforms to 2031 [3].
Key takeaway: the bill still has to be passed by the councillors. It will then go back to the lower house, which has the final say and has six days at most to decide [1][4].

So the budget combines a gesture for employees, who will pay less income tax, with an effort asked of large fuel distributors [1]. The opposition, for its part, believes too many reforms are being put off [3].
Morocco is one of France's leading economic partners in Africa. The budget sets the tax rules for the many French companies based there.
